US central bank cuts rates again as jobs market cools

Published 2026-10-07 19:15 UTC

The US central bank has cut interest rates for the third time this year as it tries to shore up a weakening jobs market. The Federal Reserve lowered its key rate by 0.25 percentage points to a range of between 3.25% and 3.5%.

In a statement, the Fed said job gains had slowed and the risks to employment had increased, though inflation remained somewhat elevated. Two officials on the rate-setting committee voted to hold rates.

Fed chair Jerome Powell said further cuts were not guaranteed and would depend on the data. The decision lowers borrowing costs for American households and businesses, and US shares rose after the announcement.

The decision means the main US interest rate now sits in a range of 3.75% to 4%. It is the third cut this year, and policymakers signalled they expect to lower borrowing costs further in the coming months if the jobs market continues to soften.

Fed chair officials said hiring had slowed sharply over the summer and that the unemployment rate had risen to its highest level in four years. At the same time, inflation has eased but remains above the central bank's 2% target, partly because of higher import prices.

The cut is likely to bring down rates on credit cards, car loans and some mortgages in the US. Savers may see lower returns on deposit accounts. Economists said lower US rates also tend to weaken the dollar, which can make US exports cheaper and affect currency markets around the world.

Not all members of the rate-setting committee agreed. Two voted against the decision, with one preferring a larger cut and another arguing that inflation risks justified keeping rates unchanged. Markets rose after the announcement, with investors betting on another cut before the end of the year.

The decision was closely watched in the UK, where the Bank of England faces its own debate about how quickly to lower rates.
